# Saṅkhapālajātaka (Ja 524)
**ID:** Ja 524
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Saṅkhapālajātaka* (Ja 524) is a canonical Jātaka tale set at Jetavana, where the Buddha recounts a story of the past to praise lay disciples observing the *uposatha* (holy day) vows, remarking that wise men of old renounced the glory of the serpent (*nāga*) world to observe these precepts [SuttaCentral]. In the narrative, which also contains references to the education of Magadhan princes at Taxila [Law 1926], the Bodhisatta is reborn as the mighty *nāga* king Saṅkhapāla [Law 1926; Bareau 1982]. Aspiring to escape the serpentine state where cultivating virtue is difficult, he leaves his luxurious underwater realm to lie upon an anthill in the human world and observe the sabbath vows, willingly offering his own body to anyone who desires it [Law 1926; Beckwith 1987; Appleton 2014]. When sixteen hunters (*Bhojaputtas*) capture, pierce, and beat him, he bears the affliction without anger, exemplifying the ultimate perfection of morality (*sīlapāramitā* or *paramattha-pāramī*), before being rescued by a passing merchant from Mithila [Law 1926; Appleton 2014; WAR YAR MEIN DA 2015].
Saṅkhapāla represents one of only three births in the Jātaka collection in which the Bodhisatta appears as a *nāga*, alongside the *Campeyyajātaka* (Ja 506) and the *Bhūridattajātaka* (Ja 543) [Scheible 2011]. All three narratives share the theme of a serpent king practicing non-violent restraint while being captured and tormented, and each is epitomized as an illustration of *sīlapāramitā* in the *Cariyāpiṭaka* (*Saṅkhapāla-cariya*) [Appleton 2014; Bareau 1982; Scheible 2011]. The legend was widely influential in Buddhist art and literature; it is depicted in the fifth-century wall paintings of Cave 1 at Ajanta, showing the *nāga* king in both serpentine and human forms [Spink 2007], and has been examined in modern philological scholarship by Thomas Oberlies in connection with the *Campeyyajātaka* [Marciniak 2019].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral connect the text to the *Vidhurajātaka* (Ja 546), the *Raṭṭhapālattheragāthā* (Thag 16.4), and the *Raṭṭhapāla Sutta* (MN 82), while noting allusions in the *Serīsakavimānavatthu* (Vv 84) and *Serīsakapetavatthu* (Pv 37) [SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse data from DharmaNexus confirms these connections, identifying direct verse sharing with Ja 546 (§27.4–30.2 ↔ §279.4–282.2), Vv 84, and Pv 37 (§27.4–30.2 ↔ §22.1–24.2), as well as significant passage-sharing with the thematic cognate *Campeyyajātaka* (§40.3–44.4 ↔ §35.4–39.4) and various commentarial works, including the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*, and *Visuddhimagga* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns several verses with Tibetan canonical collections, including the Tibetan *Jātakamālā* [DharmaNexus].
